articles.title: Pitch, notes and octaves
articles.summary: How sound becomes notes: frequency, the 12-note system, octaves and why the same note sounds different on every instrument.

body.text: Pitch is how high or low a sound is. Physically it is frequency: how many times per second the air vibrates, measured in hertz (Hz). A low bass note might vibrate 41 times a second, a whistle several thousand. Modern tuning fixes the A above middle C at 440 Hz, and every other note is tuned relative to it.

Western music divides each octave into 12 notes: C, C#/Db, D, D#/Eb, E, F, F#/Gb, G, G#/Ab, A, A#/Bb, B. On a piano the white keys are the natural notes (A to G) and the black keys are the sharps (#, one step up) and flats (b, one step down). C# and Db are the same key with two names; these are called enharmonic spellings. The distance between two neighbouring keys is a semitone (half step); two semitones make a whole step (tone). E to F and B to C are semitones with no black key between them.

An octave is the distance from one note to the next note with the same name. Going up an octave doubles the frequency: A3 is 220 Hz, A4 is 440 Hz, A5 is 880 Hz. Because the ratio is so simple, notes an octave apart sound like the same note in a higher or lower voice. The number after the letter (scientific pitch notation) tells you which octave you are in. Middle C is C4. A standard 88-key piano runs from A0 (27.5 Hz) to C8 (about 4186 Hz).

body.text: Timbre: why a piano and a violin differ on the same note

A real instrument never plays a single pure frequency. It plays a fundamental (the note you name) plus a stack of quieter overtones called harmonics, at 2x, 3x, 4x, 5x the fundamental and so on. The mix and loudness of those harmonics, and how they change over the life of the note, is the instrument's timbre or tone colour. A flute is close to a pure tone with few harmonics; a trumpet or a sawtooth synth is rich in them. The harmonic series is also where intervals come from: the 2nd harmonic is the octave, the 3rd is the fifth above that, the 5th is a major third.

Twelve-tone equal temperament, the tuning used on almost all modern instruments, makes every semitone exactly the same size so you can play in any key. Many traditions use other tunings: Arabic and Turkish maqam music uses notes between the piano keys (quarter tones and other microtones), Indian classical music uses shrutis, and blues singers bend notes between minor and major thirds. Those in-between pitches are part of each style's flavour.

Flow Music tip: Lyria responds to register and colour words more reliably than to frequencies. Say 'deep low-register', 'mid-range', 'high and airy' or 'sub' and name the instrument doing it. If you want a non-Western tuning, name the tradition, for example 'Arabic maqam melody with quarter-tone inflections'.

articles.title: Intervals
articles.summary: The distance between two notes, how each one feels, and how to use interval words in a prompt.

body.text: An interval is the distance between two notes, counted in semitones. When the notes sound one after another it is a melodic interval; when they sound together it is a harmonic interval. Intervals are the atoms of music: every melody is a chain of intervals and every chord is a stack of them.

Intervals get a number and a quality. The number counts letter names (C to E is a 3rd because it spans C, D, E). The quality tells you the exact size: major, minor, perfect, augmented or diminished. Unisons, 4ths, 5ths and octaves are called perfect because they are so stable. 2nds, 3rds, 6ths and 7ths come in major and minor versions.

body.text: Consonance and dissonance

items: Very stable (perfect consonances): unison, octave, perfect 5th, perfect 4th. They sound fused and solid, which is why power chords and drones use them.
Sweet (imperfect consonances): major and minor 3rds and 6ths. Most harmony and almost all two-part vocal harmony lives here.
Mild dissonance: major 2nd and minor 7th. They add colour and motion, typical of jazz, soul and sus chords.
Strong dissonance: minor 2nd, tritone and major 7th played together. They create tension that wants to resolve, perfect for suspense, horror and the moment before a drop.

body.text: Hearing intervals in melodies

items: Rising perfect 4th: sounds like a call to attention, a bugle or a wedding march opening.
Rising perfect 5th: heroic, wide, a classic opening for adventure and space themes.
Rising octave: a big emotional leap; singers use it to launch a chorus.
Falling minor 3rd: the playground taunt and the cuckoo call; simple and childlike.
Rising major 6th: warm and romantic, common at the start of old ballads.
Alternating minor 2nd: the slow, menacing creep of shark and horror themes.
Rising minor 6th then falling back a half step: an instant sense of longing.

body.text: Intervals invert: flip the two notes and a 3rd becomes a 6th, a 2nd becomes a 7th and a 4th becomes a 5th. The two always add up to nine (3 + 6, 2 + 7, 4 + 5). Major inverts to minor and perfect stays perfect. This is why a C major chord still sounds major whether E or G is on top.

articles.title: Major and minor keys and the circle of fifths
articles.summary: What a key is, relative and parallel keys, key signatures, the circle of fifths and why producers care.

body.text: A key is a home base. It names a tonic (the home note that feels like rest) and a scale (the set of notes that sound at home with it). A song in C major uses mostly the white keys and keeps returning to C. Major keys tend to sound bright and settled; minor keys sound darker, more serious or more emotional. That is a strong tendency, not a law: fast minor-key dance music can feel euphoric and slow major-key ballads can feel heartbreaking.

Every major key has a relative minor that uses exactly the same notes, starting three semitones lower (on the 6th degree of the major scale). C major and A minor share all seven notes; which one you are in depends on which note feels like home. A parallel minor shares the tonic instead: C major and C minor start on the same note but use different notes. Switching to the relative key is a soft mood shift; switching to the parallel key is a dramatic one.

A key signature is the list of sharps or flats a key needs. Sharps are always added in the order F C G D A E B, and flats in the reverse order B E A D G C F. So a key with two sharps always has F# and C#.
The circle of fifths

Arrange the 12 keys so each step clockwise goes up a perfect fifth: C, G, D, A, E, B, F#, then round through the flat keys Db, Ab, Eb, Bb, F and back to C. Each clockwise step adds one sharp (or removes one flat). Keys next to each other on the circle share six of their seven notes, so moving between neighbours sounds smooth, while jumping across the circle sounds dramatic. Chords also love to move counterclockwise around the circle (D to G to C), which is why ii-V-I and other fifth-based progressions feel so natural.

body.text: Why some keys feel like certain genres

items: Guitar music (rock, country, folk, punk) favours E, A, D and G because open strings ring out in those keys. Metal often tunes down to D, C or lower for weight.
Horn-driven jazz, soul, funk and big band favour flat keys (F, Bb, Eb, Ab) because trumpets, saxes and clarinets are pitched in Bb and Eb.
Piano ballads and gospel often sit in flat keys like Db, Eb and Ab, which lie comfortably under the hands on the black keys.
Electronic and hip-hop producers often choose a key that puts the bass and kick in the sweet spot: F, F#, G and A minor keep 808s and sub bass around 43 to 55 Hz.
In equal temperament every key has the same internal sound; differences come from instrument ranges, open strings and vocal range, so pick the key that suits the singer.

body.text: DJ keys: the Camelot wheel

DJs mix in key using the Camelot wheel, which relabels the circle of fifths as numbers 1 to 12 with A for minor and B for major. C major is 8B, A minor is 8A. Tracks with the same number, or one number apart, blend without clashing. Many DJ apps print Camelot codes next to the BPM.

Flow Music tip: Name the key and mode in the tempo-and-rhythm part of your prompt, e.g. 'in F# minor at 140 BPM'. Lyria treats it as a strong hint. When you extend a track or generate parts you plan to layer, keep the same key and BPM in every prompt so the pieces fit together.

articles.title: Scales
articles.summary: The note sets that give each style its colour, with formulas, moods and the genres that use them.

body.text: A scale is a set of notes arranged from low to high inside one octave. The key tells you the home note; the scale tells you which other notes belong. Scales are written as formulas, either as steps (W for a whole step, H for a half step) or as numbered degrees compared to the major scale. The major scale is W W H W W W H, or 1 2 3 4 5 6 7. A b in front of a degree means one semitone lower, a # means one higher.

Because each scale leaves out some notes and keeps others, it has a built-in mood. Pentatonic scales leave out the two most tense notes, so almost anything you play sounds pleasant, which is why they power folk tunes, blues solos and pop hooks. Harmonic minor raises one note to create an exotic, dramatic leap. Symmetrical scales like whole tone and diminished have no clear home, so they float or unsettle.

articles.title: Modes
articles.summary: The seven modes of the major scale, from brightest to darkest, and how to make each one sound like itself.

body.text: A mode is a scale built by starting the major scale on a different note. Play only the white keys from D to D and you get Dorian; from E to E is Phrygian; from F to F is Lydian; from G to G is Mixolydian; from A to A is Aeolian (natural minor); from B to B is Locrian; from C to C is Ionian (major). Same notes, different home, completely different mood.

The easiest way to hear modes is to compare each one to the major scale on the same root. Each mode changes one or more notes, and the most distinctive changed note is its characteristic note. Ordered from brightest to darkest, each mode lowers one more note than the last: Lydian, Ionian, Mixolydian, Dorian, Aeolian, Phrygian, Locrian.

body.text: A chord is three or more notes sounding together. Most chords are built by stacking thirds on top of a root: root, 3rd and 5th make a triad; add the 7th and you have a seventh chord; keep stacking (9th, 11th, 13th) and you get extended chords. The 3rd decides major or minor; the 7th adds colour and pull; extensions add richness.

body.text: Voicing and voice leading

Voicing is how you spread a chord's notes. Close voicings pack notes tightly (warm, dense, piano-like). Open or spread voicings space them over two octaves (orchestral, cinematic, airy). Shell voicings play only root, 3rd and 7th (jazz guitar and piano comping). Rootless voicings leave the root to the bass player. Voice leading means moving each note to the nearest note of the next chord, so chords connect smoothly like separate singers. Good voice leading is why a simple progression can sound expensive.

Put the chord instrument and the chord colour together.

articles.title: Chord progressions
articles.summary: The progressions behind most popular music, written in Roman numerals with examples, moods and genres.

body.text: A chord progression is the order in which chords change. Writing it in Roman numerals (I, IV, V) instead of letter names lets you move it to any key. Uppercase is major, lowercase is minor, ° is diminished, and a b in front means the chord's root is borrowed a semitone lower than the key's own note (bVII in C is Bb). Examples below are in C major or A minor.

Chords have jobs. Tonic chords (I, vi, sometimes iii) feel like home. Predominant chords (ii, IV) move away. Dominant chords (V, vii°) create tension that wants to resolve home. Most progressions cycle home, away, tension, home. Loops that never fully resolve (vi-IV-I-V, i-bVI) keep listeners leaning forward, which is why they dominate modern pop and hip-hop.

articles.summary: Beats, bars, note values, time signatures, syncopation, swing, triplets and polyrhythm explained for producers.

body.text: Rhythm is how sounds are placed in time. The beat (or pulse) is the steady tick you tap your foot to. Beats group into bars (measures), and the time signature tells you how many beats each bar has and which note value counts as one beat. In 4/4, by far the most common meter, there are four quarter-note beats per bar. Beat 1 is the downbeat; beats 2 and 4 are the backbeat, where the snare usually hits in pop, rock and hip-hop.

body.text: Syncopation

Syncopation means accenting the weak parts of the beat: the 'ands' and the 'e's and 'a's between the beats. It creates push and surprise. An anticipation (or push) is a note that arrives a little early, usually an eighth or sixteenth before the downbeat, which makes a chord change feel urgent. The most important syncopated cell in modern music is the tresillo, 3+3+2: three hits spread across eight sixteenths as 'x..x..x.'. It powers reggaeton, dancehall, Afrobeats, moombahton and countless pop choruses.
Swing and shuffle

Swing turns pairs of even notes into long-short pairs. At full triplet swing the first note of each pair takes two thirds of the beat and the second takes one third. Drum machines and DAWs express swing as a percentage: 50% is straight, about 66% is triplet shuffle, and the subtle 54 to 62% range is the famous head-nodding swing of hip-hop and house. Swing can be applied to eighths (jazz, blues shuffle) or sixteenths (funk, boom bap, garage).
Triplets, hemiola and polyrhythm

Triplets squeeze three notes into the space of two. Playing a triplet pattern over a straight beat creates three-against-two, the basic polyrhythm of African, Afro-Cuban and Afro-Brazilian music. When the music briefly regroups 6 beats as 3+3 instead of 2+2+2, that is hemiola, common in Baroque music and Latin styles. Polyrhythm layers different subdivisions (3 against 4, 5 against 4) at the same time; polymeter layers loops of different lengths, like a 3-beat synth riff cycling over a 4-beat drum loop, which drifts in and out of alignment and drives a lot of techno and minimal music.

articles.title: Tempo and BPM by genre
articles.summary: How fast music is, how fast every major genre usually runs, and the half-time and double-time tricks that change how a tempo feels.

body.text: Tempo is the speed of the beat, measured in beats per minute (BPM). 60 BPM is one beat per second, roughly a resting heartbeat; 120 BPM is a brisk walk; 174 BPM is a sprint. Tempo is one of the strongest genre signals there is: the same drums at 90 BPM say hip-hop and at 174 BPM say drum and bass.

Feel matters as much as the number. A trap beat at 140 BPM has its snare on beat 3 instead of 2 and 4, so it feels like 70 BPM: that is half-time. Drum and bass at 174 often has a half-time section that feels like 87. Double-time is the opposite: a 90 BPM hip-hop beat with sixteenth-note hats and a rapid flow feels like 180. When you write a BPM for genres with half-time feels, write the number the genre normally uses (140 for trap, 174 for drum and bass) and add 'half-time feel' if you want it.

articles.title: Melody and hooks
articles.summary: What makes a melody memorable: contour, steps and leaps, motifs, phrasing and the many kinds of hook.

body.text: A melody is a line of single notes with rhythm: the part you hum. It has a contour (its shape: rising, falling, arching or zigzagging), a range (lowest to highest note), and a rhythm. Melodies move by steps (to the neighbouring note, called conjunct motion) and leaps (jumps of a 3rd or more, called disjunct motion). Steps feel smooth and conversational; leaps feel dramatic and emotional. Good melodies mix them, and a common rule of thumb is that a big leap is followed by a step back in the opposite direction, which feels like the tune catching its balance.

Melodies are built from small ideas. A motif is a short cell of two to five notes with a distinctive rhythm. Composers repeat it, move it up or down (a sequence), flip it upside down (inversion), play it backwards (retrograde), stretch it (augmentation) or squeeze it (diminution). A phrase is a musical sentence, often two or four bars long. Phrases often come in pairs: a question (antecedent) that ends open, and an answer (consequent) that ends at home.
Principles of a strong melody

items: Keep verses lower and narrower, then lift the chorus higher and wider. The jump in register is what makes a chorus feel like a payoff.
Repeat more than you think. Most hooks repeat a short idea three times and change it the fourth time.
Give it a rhythm people could clap. A melody with a distinctive rhythm is recognisable even when hummed on one note.
Land on chord tones (root, 3rd, 5th) on strong beats; use passing and tension notes on weak beats.
Leave space. Rests let the listener breathe and give call-and-response parts room to answer.
Use one surprise: an unexpected leap, a held tension note, a blue note or a syncopated entry.
Pentatonic melodies are the easiest to sing and the hardest to make sound wrong, which is why so many global hooks use them.

body.text: Ornament and expression

Melodies come alive through ornaments: grace notes (quick notes before the main note), slides into notes, trills (rapid alternation with the neighbour note), turns, mordents, vocal runs and melisma (many notes on one syllable, central to gospel and R&B), and blue notes (pitches bent between minor and major). Each tradition has its own: Irish fiddle cuts and rolls, Indian gamakas, Arabic and Turkish trills and slides, country yodel breaks.

body.text: Once you know the diatonic chords of a key, the interesting part is breaking the rules on purpose. These are the tricks composers and producers use to add surprise, emotion and lift without losing the listener.

body.text: Key changes in practice

A modulation is a change of key. The simplest is direct modulation: just jump. A pivot chord that belongs to both keys makes the move smoother. A dominant chord of the new key (V7 of the new key just before it arrives) makes the arrival feel inevitable. Upward key changes for a final chorus add excitement; moving down a step or into a flat key (C to Ab) feels like a warm sunset or a reflective turn.
Pedal tones and drones

A pedal tone is a note held or repeated in the bass while chords change above it. It builds tension because some chords clash with it, then release as harmony returns to agree with the bass. EDM builds, cinematic swells and rock intros all lean on pedals. A drone is a long-held pedal, central to Indian classical music (the tanpura), bagpipes, ambient music and drone metal.
Suspensions and appoggiaturas

A suspension holds a note from the previous chord into the next, creating a brief dissonance that then resolves down a step. The sus4 to major move is the pop version. An appoggiatura is a dissonant note that lands on a strong beat and resolves by step; it is one of the most reliable ways to create a lump-in-the-throat moment, and singers use it instinctively on emotional words.

articles.title: Song structure and arrangement
articles.summary: Sections and their jobs, common forms, the energy curve, layering, call and response and arrangement moves that keep a track alive.

body.text: Structure is the order of sections; arrangement is what plays in each section and how it changes. Listeners stay engaged when every section has a clear job and each one differs from the last in at least one obvious way: drums enter or drop out, the register lifts, a new instrument arrives, the rhythm switches.

body.text: Common forms

items: Verse-chorus pop: Intro, Verse 1, Pre-Chorus, Chorus, Verse 2, Pre-Chorus, Chorus, Bridge, Final Chorus, Outro. About 3 minutes, first chorus by 0:45.
AABA (32-bar song form): two verses, a contrasting bridge, a final verse. The classic jazz standard and early pop shape.
Strophic: the same music repeated with new words (A A A). Folk songs, hymns, ballads.
12-bar blues: repeating 12-bar choruses; lyrics often follow AAB (a line, repeated, then an answer).
Hip-hop: Intro, Hook, Verse (16 bars), Hook, Verse (16 bars), Hook, Outro. Hooks are often 8 bars.
EDM: Intro, Build, Drop, Breakdown, Build, Drop, Outro. Sections are multiples of 8 or 16 bars so DJs can mix.
Through-composed: music keeps evolving with no returning sections. Film cues, art songs, ambient.

body.text: The energy curve

Plot energy over time and most hits look like a staircase with a dip near the end: the intro is low, verse 1 is a little higher, the pre-chorus climbs, chorus 1 peaks, verse 2 comes down but sits higher than verse 1, chorus 2 peaks higher, the bridge or breakdown drops right down, and the final chorus is the biggest moment of the song. Electronic tracks do the same with build and drop cycles. The dip before the final peak matters: contrast is what makes the last chorus feel huge.

rows: hats, shakers, percussion, rhythm guitar, comping keys

body.text: A useful rule: at any moment, only one thing should be the star, and roughly three to five elements should be clearly audible. Each section can add or remove one layer. Many great arrangements save one instrument for the final chorus so it feels new.
Call and response

Call and response is a phrase answered by another phrase: a lead vocal answered by a choir, a vocal line answered by a guitar lick, a synth stab answered by a horn hit. It comes from African and African-American traditions (work songs, gospel, blues) and runs through jazz, funk, Latin music, hip-hop ad-libs and pop. It fills the gaps in a melody and makes a track feel like a conversation.
Arrangement moves that keep listeners hooked

items: Drop the drums for the last bar of the pre-chorus so the chorus downbeat hits harder.
Double or stack the lead vocal in the chorus; keep the verse single and dry.
Switch the hi-hats from eighths to sixteenths when the chorus arrives.
Use a half-time bridge to make the return to full time feel like a launch.
Introduce a counter-melody in the second verse so it differs from the first.
End on a stripped-down version of the hook for an intimate outro.

body.text: Dynamics are the loudness levels of music and how they change. Expression covers everything else a performer does to make notes feel alive: articulation (how notes start and end), timing (pushing or relaxing the tempo), tone colour and intensity. A machine-perfect performance at one volume sounds flat; dynamics and expression are what make music breathe.

body.text: Dynamics in modern production

In electronic production dynamics show up as velocity (how hard a MIDI note is struck, 1 to 127), automation (volume and filter moves over time) and arrangement (adding and removing layers). Compression and limiting reduce the difference between loud and soft; heavy compression sounds powerful and in-your-face but can flatten emotion, while light compression keeps an open, breathing, acoustic feel. Genres differ: classical and jazz recordings keep wide dynamics, while EDM, trap and modern pop are dense and loud from start to finish, relying on arrangement contrast instead.

body.text: Bass is the bridge between rhythm and harmony. It plays the lowest notes, which tell the ear what each chord really is, and it locks rhythmically with the kick drum to create groove. A bass line can make the same chords sound like reggae, disco, funk or trap. Its fundamental notes sit roughly between 30 and 250 Hz: a 4-string bass's low E is 41 Hz, a 5-string's low B is 31 Hz, and 808s and sub basses often sit between 35 and 60 Hz.

body.text: Bass and kick

The kick and bass both live in the low end, so they must cooperate. In trap the 808 often is the kick and bass at once, so a separate kick is short and clicky.

Almost every synth follows the same chain: a sound source (oscillator, sample or noise) produces raw tone, a filter shapes its brightness, an amplifier controls its loudness, and modulators (envelopes and LFOs) move those settings over time so the sound plucks, swells, wobbles or evolves. body.text: Analog, digital and software

Analog synths use continuously varying voltages; their slight instabilities (oscillator drift, filter saturation) give a warm, alive feel. Digital synths compute sound with numbers; they can do things analog cannot (FM, wavetables, huge polyphony) and sound clean or glassy. Virtual analog digitally imitates analog circuits. Software synths (plugins) run in a DAW and today cover every style. A synth is monophonic if it plays one note at a time (classic for basses and leads), polyphonic if it plays chords, and paraphonic if it plays several pitches through one shared filter and amp.

body.text: Subtractive synthesis is the classic analog approach and the foundation of most synth sounds you know. You start with a harmonically rich oscillator, usually a sawtooth or square, and subtract harmonics with a filter. Envelopes then move the filter and volume over time, and LFOs add motion. It is called subtractive because you remove, rather than build, the tone colour.

Mono legato mode only re-triggers envelopes when you lift your fingers, which gives smooth slurred lines. Glide (portamento) makes pitch slide between notes; it is the secret of the whining synth leads of 1990s West Coast hip-hop and the sliding basses of acid. Keyboard tracking makes the filter open as you play higher, so notes stay evenly bright. Velocity, aftertouch and the mod wheel let you play dynamics and vibrato in real time.

body.text: An envelope is a shape that a parameter follows every time you press a key. The standard envelope has four stages, ADSR: Attack (how long it takes to rise to full level), Decay (how long it takes to fall to the sustain level), Sustain (the level held while the key stays down, a level not a time) and Release (how long it takes to fade after the key is released). The amp envelope shapes loudness; the filter envelope shapes brightness. Most of a sound's identity, pluck or pad or stab, comes from its envelopes.

body.text: Amp envelope versus filter envelope

The two envelopes work together. A pluck often has a short amp decay and an even shorter filter decay, so the note starts bright and immediately darkens. A pad might have a slow amp attack and a slow filter attack, so it fades in and gradually brightens. Envelope amount sets how far the filter envelope opens the filter; velocity can scale it so harder playing is brighter. The TB-303 adds an accent that briefly boosts both volume and filter, which is part of its squelch.

body.text: Static sounds are boring. Modulation is anything that changes a parameter automatically. The most common modulator is the LFO, a low-frequency oscillator running below hearing (roughly 0.01 to 20 Hz) whose waveform moves a parameter up and down. A sine LFO gives smooth wobbles; a square flips between two values; a sawtooth ramps; sample-and-hold (S&H) jumps to random values, the classic 'computer bloop' sound.

body.text: Tempo sync

Synced LFOs lock to the song's tempo, which turns modulation into rhythm. A filter LFO at 1/4 notes pulses with the beat; 1/8 triplets give a swung wobble; switching between 1/4, 1/8 and 1/16 inside a phrase is the heart of dubstep wobble bass. Free-running (unsynced) LFOs drift across the beat and feel organic, which suits pads and ambient music.

articles.title: FM synthesis
articles.summary: Carriers, modulators, ratios and the DX7: how frequency modulation creates bells, electric pianos and metallic basses.

body.text: FM (frequency modulation) synthesis makes complex tones by using one oscillator to wobble the pitch of another at audio speed. The oscillator you hear is the carrier; the one wobbling it is the modulator. FM synths call each oscillator an operator. The ratio between modulator and carrier frequency decides whether the result is harmonic (musical, like a saw or square) or inharmonic (bell-like, metallic). The modulation index, how strongly the modulator acts, decides brightness. An envelope on the modulator's level makes the brightness change over each note, which is how FM imitates the bright attack and mellow decay of real instruments.
The DX7 and its descendants

Yamaha's DX7 (1983) brought FM to the masses with six operators arranged in 32 algorithms (patterns of which operators modulate which). Its glassy electric piano, bells, marimbas, slap-like basses and sharp brass became the sound of 1980s ballads, city pop, R&B and new jack swing. FM chips (like Yamaha's YM2612) also powered 16-bit game consoles, giving their music a punchy, metallic character. Modern FM instruments include Elektron Digitone, Korg opsix, Yamaha Montage, Native Instruments FM8 and Ableton Operator. Modern bass music uses FM for aggressive growls and neuro basses.

articles.title: Wavetable synthesis
articles.summary: Scanning and morphing through tables of waveforms: the engine behind modern EDM basses and evolving pads.

body.text: A wavetable is a series of single-cycle waveforms (frames) stored in order, often 256 of them. Instead of playing one waveform, the oscillator can move through the table, morphing from one shape to the next. Modulating the wavetable position with an envelope or LFO makes the timbre move: a pad that opens from soft to glassy, a bass that talks, a lead that snarls. Wavetables can be drawn, generated from maths or made from any sample, including voices and real instruments.

body.text: Warp modes

Modern wavetable synths add warp modes that bend the waveform further: sync (hard-sync sweeps), bend (squeeze the wave), mirror, PWM-style asymmetry, FM from another oscillator, and remap. Combine them with movement and distortion and you get the talking 'yoi', growl and riddim basses of dubstep and the shimmering chords of future bass.

articles.title: Additive synthesis
articles.summary: Building sounds from individual sine-wave partials, from drawbar organs to spectral resynthesis.

body.text: Additive synthesis builds a sound by adding together many sine waves (partials), each with its own frequency and level. In theory any sound can be made this way, because every sound is a sum of sine waves (Fourier's principle). A sawtooth is all harmonics with levels falling as 1/n; a square is only the odd harmonics. The Hammond organ is a mechanical additive synth: each drawbar adds one harmonic, which is why organists talk about registrations like '888000000'.

body.text: Because you control every partial, additive is excellent for glassy pads, choral tones, bells and spectral morphing, and for resynthesis: analysing a recorded sound and rebuilding it from partials so you can stretch, morph or blur it. The downside is complexity: real sounds need dozens to hundreds of partials, each moving. Instruments such as the Kawai K5000, Image-Line Harmor, Native Instruments Razor and the additive engines in Arturia Pigments make this manageable with spectral filters and morphing.

Flow Music tip: Additive results are best described as 'organ-like', 'glassy', 'choral', 'spectral' or 'bell-like'. For organs, name the instrument and registration feel: 'full Hammond drawbars', 'soft flute-stop organ'.

body.text: Granular synthesis slices a sample into tiny pieces called grains, typically 1 to 100 milliseconds long, and plays many of them at once, overlapping, from chosen positions in the sample. Because the grains are independent, you can freeze a moment in time, stretch a sound without changing pitch, change pitch without changing speed, or scatter grains into a shimmering cloud. A single vocal syllable or piano note becomes an endless pad.

body.text: A sampler records or loads audio and plays it back from a keyboard or pads. A sample can be a one-shot (a single drum hit or note) or a loop (a bar of drums, a chord progression). Samplers map samples across key zones and velocity layers, use round robins (alternating samples) to stop repeated notes sounding robotic, and set loop points so short samples can sustain. Pitching a sample up on a vintage sampler also speeds it up, which is where the chipmunk-soul sound comes from; modern samplers can time-stretch to change speed and pitch independently.

body.text: Unison stacks several copies of the same voice for each note, each slightly detuned and spread across the stereo field. The copies drift in and out of phase, creating a thick, wide, shimmering sound. Detune controls how far apart the copies are: a little sounds fat and analog; a lot sounds huge, sour or rave-like. Spread controls how wide they pan.

body.text: The supersaw and its relatives

The supersaw is a single oscillator made of seven detuned sawtooths, introduced on the Roland JP-8000 (1996). It became the defining lead and chord sound of trance and later of festival EDM and future bass. The Reese bass, two slightly detuned saws through a low-pass filter, gives drum and bass its moving, phasing low end. The hoover, created on Roland's Alpha Juno synths, combines detuned pulse waves, PWM and a pitch dive; it is the menacing whine of early-90s rave and hardcore.
Chorus and ensemble

Chorus is a cheaper way to similar width: the signal is copied, delayed by a few milliseconds and the delay time is wobbled by an LFO. The built-in chorus on Roland Juno synths is part of their famous warmth. String machines use a three-phase ensemble chorus for their lush shimmer. Chorus on clean guitar defines much of 1980s and dream-pop guitar.
Keep the low end mono

Wide unison sounds can disappear when a mix is played in mono (phones, club systems), because detuned copies cancel. Producers often keep the bass centred and mono below about 100 to 150 Hz and let unison width live above that, or use a separate mono sub layer under a wide supersaw bass.

body.text: How drums are recorded

A studio kit might use a dozen microphones: close mics on each drum for punch and detail, overheads above the kit for the cymbals and overall picture, and room mics further away for size and ambience. Heavily compressed room mics give the explosive drum sound of 1970s and 1980s rock; tight close mics with little room give dry, punchy 1970s funk and soul. The ratio of close to room sound is one of the biggest cues for era and genre.

body.text: Drum machines started as organ accessories playing preset rhythms like 'waltz' and 'bossa nova'. Many of the most famous machines were commercial flops at first; cheap second-hand prices put them in the hands of young producers who used them in ways their makers never intended.

articles.title: Groove, swing, ghost notes and feel
articles.summary: What makes a beat feel good: swing percentages, ghost notes, playing ahead of or behind the beat, and the feels that define genres.

body.text: Groove is the quality that makes you move. Two beats with the same notes can feel stiff or irresistible depending on tiny details: how much the off-beats are delayed (swing), how loud each hit is (dynamics and accents), whether quiet notes fill the gaps (ghost notes) and whether parts sit slightly ahead of or behind the grid (push and pull). 'The pocket' is the sweet spot where drums and bass lock together and the groove feels inevitable.
Swing

Swing delays every second subdivision. In a DAW or drum machine it is shown as a percentage: 50 percent is perfectly straight, about 66 percent is a full triplet shuffle, and 75 percent is extreme. The sweet spot for hip-hop, house and garage is often 54 to 62 percent applied to sixteenths, a subtle lilt that makes hats and percussion bounce. Jazz and blues swing eighth notes much harder, near triplet feel, with the ride cymbal playing 'ding, ding-a ding'.
Ghost notes and dynamics

Ghost notes are very quiet snare hits between the main backbeats, felt more than heard. They are the secret of funk, R&B, neo-soul and gospel drumming. Accents work the other way: some hits are louder to shape the phrase. Hi-hats with alternating loud and soft strokes sound human; hi-hats at one velocity sound mechanical. Most drum machines and DAWs call this velocity (1 to 127).

Behind the beat (laid back): relaxed, heavy, cool. Neo-soul, boom bap, reggae, slow R&B.
Drunken or unquantized: each instrument drifts a little differently, kick early, snare late. The off-kilter swing of neo-soul and modern beat-scene hip-hop.

articles.title: 808s and sub bass tuning
articles.summary: How the 808 kick became a bass instrument, how to tune it to the key, and how 808s and kicks share the low end.

body.text: The Roland TR-808's kick is a decaying sine wave with a short pitch drop at the start. Turn up its decay and it rings for seconds, becoming a deep bass note. Hip-hop producers discovered they could tune this '808' to play bass lines, and modern trap, drill and much of pop is built on it. Today '808' means any long, tuned, sine-based bass hit, often sampled, distorted and pitched across the keyboard.
Tune it to the key

Because an 808 is a pitched note, it must match the song's key or it will clash with the chords. Producers tune the root of the 808 to the tonic or play the 808 as a bass line following the chord roots. Most 808s sound best with their fundamental between about 40 and 60 Hz: low enough to feel, high enough to be heard on decent speakers.

body.text: Making 808s hit on every speaker

items: Phone and laptop speakers barely reproduce anything below 80 to 100 Hz. Saturation and distortion add harmonics an octave or more above the fundamental, so the ear still hears the bass line.
Keep the 808 mono and centred; stereo width in the sub region causes problems in clubs and in mono playback.
Match decay to tempo: long decays fill space in slow, sparse beats; short decays keep fast patterns from smearing.
Glides (portamento) between 808 notes are a trap and drill signature. Slides of a fifth or an octave are common.
Watch the pitch envelope: a strong initial drop gives punch; too much makes the note feel out of tune.

body.text: 808 versus sub bass versus bass guitar

An 808 has a hit-like attack and a decaying tail; a sub bass is a sustained sine that holds as long as the note does (dubstep, grime, UK garage); a bass guitar has rich mid-range harmonics and fingers or a pick on the attack. In prompts, these three words lead to three very different low ends.

body.text: Programmed drums can sound stiff or sensational. The difference comes from a handful of habits that experienced producers apply almost automatically. Drum patterns are often written as 16 steps per bar, one character per sixteenth note: x for a hit, X for an accent, o for a ghost note, a dot for silence. Steps 1, 5, 9 and 13 are the four beats. FLOWSMITH's beat patterns use this notation.

Some vintage EQs are loved for colour as much as control. The Pultec EQP-1A tube EQ gives silky low and high shelves; boosting and cutting the same low frequency at once creates its famous tight, deep low end. The Neve 1073 preamp EQ adds thick, musical warmth. API 550 EQs are punchy and forward. SSL console EQs are clean and aggressive. Plugin emulations of all of them are everywhere.

articles.summary: How compressors control dynamics and add punch, the main controls, classic compressor types and techniques like parallel and bus compression.

body.text: A compressor automatically turns a sound down when it gets louder than a set level (the threshold). This reduces the difference between loud and soft parts (dynamic range), which makes a performance more even, lets you raise the overall level, and, depending on settings, adds punch, sustain, density or glue. Overdone, it sounds squashed, pumping and lifeless; used well, it is the sound of polished records.

body.text: Sidechaining means a compressor (or volume tool) reacts to a different sound from the one it is processing. The classic setup: a compressor on the bass listens to the kick, so every time the kick hits, the bass dips briefly. The kick punches through clearly and the low end stays clean. Push it further on pads, chords or the whole mix and you get the rhythmic 'breathing' or 'pumping' that defines French house, EDM, future bass and much modern pop.

body.text: Reverb is the dense wash of reflections you hear after a sound in a space. It tells the brain how big the room is and how far away the sound is. Dry sounds feel close and modern; wet sounds feel distant, dreamy or grand. Early recordings captured real rooms; later engineers used echo chambers, metal plates, springs and finally digital algorithms and convolution (recordings of real spaces).

body.text: Creating depth

A mix has three dimensions: left-right (panning), up-down (frequency) and front-back (depth). To bring something forward: keep it drier, brighter and louder. To push something back: add more reverb, roll off highs, lower its level. Putting all instruments in one shared reverb space makes them sound like a band in a room; giving the lead vocal its own shorter, brighter plate makes it stand in front.

A single short repeat thickens or adds a rockabilly slap; many repeats (feedback) create rhythmic echoes; long, filtered, modulated echoes create space and atmosphere. Because echoes are rhythmic, delay times are usually synced to the tempo.

body.text: Saturation and distortion add harmonics by pushing a signal harder than a circuit can cleanly handle. A little sounds warm, thick and 'analog'; more sounds gritty; a lot sounds fuzzy, broken or aggressive. Distortion also makes sounds seem louder and helps bass and 808s be heard on small speakers, because it generates higher harmonics of low notes.

body.text: Tips

items: Parallel distortion: blend a heavily distorted copy under the clean sound for grit without losing body.
Distort before or after the filter for different results: before is smoother, after is nastier.
Distort the mids of a bass, not the sub: split the bass and keep the sub clean.
Saturation on the drum bus adds glue and loudness; on vocals it adds presence and attitude.
Even harmonics (tube, tape) sound musical and warm; odd harmonics (hard clipping, fuzz) sound edgy and aggressive.

articles.title: Stereo width and panning
articles.summary: Placing sounds left to right, mono compatibility, mid/side processing and making mixes feel wide or intimate.

body.text: Panning places each sound between the left and right speakers. Stereo width is how spread a sound or a whole mix feels. A well-panned mix has a solid centre (kick, snare, bass, lead vocal) and supporting parts spread to the sides, so everything is heard clearly. Width also creates emotion: intimate songs often feel narrow and close; anthems and ambient pieces feel vast.

Typical placement
Notes

body.text: Width tools

items: Double-tracking: recording a part twice and panning the takes apart. The most natural width.
Haas effect: a very short delay (under about 30 ms) on one side makes a sound feel wide.
Chorus and unison: detuned copies spread across the field.
Mid/side processing: adjusting the centre (mid) and the sides separately, for example brightening the sides to widen.
Stereo reverb and ping-pong delay: put the space around the sound.
LCR mixing: panning only hard left, centre or hard right, for a bold, clear, classic sound.

body.text: Mono compatibility

Many listeners hear music in mono: phone speakers, smart speakers, some club systems. Over-widened sounds can partly cancel in mono and disappear. Engineers keep the sub and bass centred, check mixes in mono, and use width selectively. Spatial audio formats like Dolby Atmos add height and surround placement for headphones and home theatres.

Flow Music tip: Width words set the scale of a track: 'wide, immersive stereo field', 'intimate, narrow and close', 'hard-panned double-tracked guitars', 'percussion swirling around the stereo field'. Use 'wide' for choruses and drops and 'intimate' for verses to create contrast.

body.text: Mastering is the final stage of production: making a finished mix sound polished, consistent and ready for every playback system. A mastering engineer listens on accurate speakers and makes subtle adjustments: broad EQ for tonal balance, gentle compression for glue, saturation for density, stereo adjustments, and limiting to reach a competitive loudness without distortion. They also sequence albums so tracks flow at consistent levels.

body.text: Streaming normalisation

Streaming services turn loud tracks down (and sometimes quiet ones up) so everything plays at similar loudness. Spotify, YouTube and Tidal normalise to about -14 LUFS, Apple Music to about -16 LUFS. That means crushing a master for extra loudness no longer wins: it just gets turned down and sounds flatter than a more dynamic master. Many engineers still master loud for genre expectations (EDM, trap, metal) but with care to keep punch.

Limiter: catch peaks and set final loudness with a true-peak ceiling.

They build tension before a chorus or drop, mark the arrival of a new section with impact, and smooth the move from one energy level to another. Electronic music uses dedicated sound effects; band music uses fills, swells and pauses. Both rely on the same ideas: rising pitch and brightness build tension, a sudden drop or hit releases it.

articles.title: Writing hooks
articles.summary: How to write a chorus people remember: title placement, repetition, contrast, prosody and singable sounds.

body.text: A hook is the part of a song that grabs attention and sticks. In most songs it is the chorus, built around the title. Strong hooks are short, repeated, rhythmically distinctive and emotionally clear. They also contrast with the verse: if the verse is low, busy and wordy, the chorus is high, open and simple.
Principles

items: Put the title in the first or last line of the chorus, ideally both.
Keep the hook phrase short: two to six words is typical.
Repeat it. A chorus that repeats its hook line two to four times is not lazy; it is how memory works.
Make the chorus melody higher, with longer notes, than the verse.
Change the rhythm: if the verse is fast and syncopated, give the chorus long held notes, or the reverse.
Use prosody: put stressed syllables on strong beats so words sound natural when sung.
Use open vowels on long, high notes: 'oh', 'ah', 'ay', 'ee' sing better than closed sounds like 'it' or 'up'.
Say one idea per chorus. The verses explain; the chorus states the feeling.

Many modern songs add a post-chorus: a short section right after the chorus with a chant, a vocal chop or an instrumental riff that repeats the hook in a new form. In electronic music the drop itself is the hook, often built from a processed vocal fragment or a lead synth melody. A whistled or hummed line can work too.

body.text: Rhyme in rap

Rap usually stacks rhymes much more densely than sung music. Rappers rhyme multiple syllables at once (multis), place rhymes inside lines as well as at the end, and chain the same vowel sound across four or eight bars before switching. End rhymes often land on beat 4 or on the snare, which gives a satisfying click. A rhyme scheme can also run across bar lines, so the rhyme lands in an unexpected place for surprise.

Flow Music tip: When you write your own lyrics, rhyme scheme and syllable count matter more to Lyria than fancy words. Consistent line lengths and clear end rhymes help it place words on the beat. In the prompt you can request a rap style, e.g. 'dense multisyllabic internal rhymes'.

articles.title: Syllables and flow for rap
articles.summary: Bars, syllables per bar, pockets and the main flow styles, with guidance on writing lines that sit on the beat.

body.text: Flow is how a rapper's words ride the beat: the rhythm of syllables, where they start and stop, where rhymes and stresses fall. A bar is one measure of 4 beats. A standard verse is 16 bars, a hook is usually 8. Each beat can be split into eighths (2 syllables per beat), sixteenths (4 per beat) or triplets (3 per beat), and the subdivision a rapper chooses defines the flow.
Writing lines that sit in the pocket

items: Count syllables. Lines in the same section should have similar syllable counts so they fit the same number of beats.
Mark the stresses. Put stressed syllables on beats and important words on beat 1 or on the snare (2 and 4).
Land rhymes on strong points: end rhymes on beat 4 or the snare feel resolved.
Leave breaths. A line that fills every sixteenth for 16 bars is exhausting and hard to generate cleanly.
Switch it up. Changing from eighths to triplets halfway through a verse is one of the most effective flow moves.
Use pickups: starting a phrase just before beat 1 (anacrusis) adds momentum.
Write ad-libs in parentheses after the main line so they read as background shouts.

body.text: Example: counting a bar

Take the line 'Late nights, city lights, I was chasing what I'm owed'. It has 13 syllables. Rapped in sixteenth notes it fills just under one bar, with 'Late', 'ci-', 'chas-' and 'owed' landing near the beats. Shorten it to 'Late nights, city lights' (6 syllables) and it becomes a punchy half-bar phrase that leaves room for an ad-lib answer.

Flow Music tip: Lyria fits your words to the beat, so consistent syllable counts per line and section give much tighter results. In the prompt, describe the flow: 'triplet flow', 'laid-back behind-the-beat delivery', 'rapid double-time verse', 'melodic Auto-Tuned rap'.
